meta.label: Video calls
meta.attribution: Built from providers' own security and pricing documentation, their terms of service, open-source repositories and the licences GitHub reports for them, all read on 2026-09-29; not measured data. Call settings change between releases, so read the current documentation before relying on a row. Privacy means whether calls are end-to-end encrypted by default, as each provider's own documentation states it. A provider that offers end-to-end encryption only as an option, or only for some room sizes, scores below one that applies it to every call, and a provider whose documentation does not settle the question is scored on what it does say. Openness reflects whether the call software or its encryption code is published and under what licence, and where the terms bar reverse engineering the row says so. For WhatsApp it rests on the European Commission's timetable requiring it to open calls to other services by September 2027, which has not yet happened. It is left empty for FaceTime, Webex and Whereby, where nothing read settled it. Accessibility covers how easily a person can start a call and how easily a guest can join without an account or an install; it says nothing about disability access, which needs its own measure. Economical reflects what the free tier allows in meeting length and group size, or the one-off price, and is left empty for FaceTime because the pages read give no price. Skype is not listed because Microsoft retired it on 5 May 2025. BigBlueButton, in the earlier shared dataset, is left out because it is classroom software that needs an institution or a paid host, so one person cannot simply start a call with it. Element Call is scored here as a calling tool; the messaging decision covers Element's chat. Suggest changes via Contribute.

criteria.label: Open source, or open to other services
Easy to start, and easy for a guest to join without an account or install
Economical, judged by what the free tier allows

products.name: Zoom (Basic plan)

privacy.note: Zoom's support page says end-to-end encryption has to be enabled in the web portal, that hosts on free accounts can use it after verifying a phone number by SMS, that every participant must join from the desktop app, mobile app or Zoom Rooms, and that turning it on disables cloud recording, live transcription, polls, Zoom AI features and several other in-meeting features.

openness.note: Zoom's terms of service prohibit customers from modifying, decompiling, reverse engineering or attempting to gain access to the source code of its services and software.

accessibility.note: Zoom's free plan page says participants can join without a Zoom account, while the host signs in to the Zoom app or web portal to host.

economical.note: Zoom's free plan page advertises free meetings of up to 40 minutes for up to 100 participants.

products.description: A mainstream meeting tool that is easy for a guest to join. Calls are end-to-end encrypted only when the host turns it on and every participant uses an app. The US FTC's 2020 settlement says Zoom had advertised end-to-end encryption while keeping the keys that let it read meetings.

products.name: Google Meet

privacy.note: Google's Meet privacy page says audio and video on 1:1 and group calls in the new Meet app are end-to-end encrypted and not stored on Google servers, and that Google does not use information in apps where people mainly store personal content, including Meet, for advertising. For features such as recordings and polls it says data is encrypted in transit and at rest.

openness.note: Google's Terms of Service, effective 30 July 2026, list reverse engineering its services or underlying technology to extract trade secrets or other proprietary information among prohibited uses, except as applicable law allows.

accessibility.note: Google's Meet page says that in the no-cost version participants can sign in with a Google Account or be approved by the meeting organizer to join, and that anyone with a Google Account can create a meeting.

economical.note: Google's Meet page says anyone with a Google Account can host up to 100 participants for up to 60 minutes per meeting at no cost, with no time limit for mobile calls and 1:1s; group calls of up to 24 hours are listed as a premium feature.

products.description: Calls in the Meet app are end-to-end encrypted, and Google says Meet content is not used for advertising. Free group meetings stop at 60 minutes, and guests need a Google Account or the organizer's approval.

products.name: FaceTime

privacy.note: Apple's Platform Security guide says FaceTime call contents are protected by end-to-end encryption so no one but the sender and receiver can access them and Apple cannot decrypt the data, and that Group FaceTime calls are end-to-end encrypted among the invited participants' devices.

accessibility.note: Apple's FaceTime requirements page says making a call requires being signed in to FaceTime with an Apple Account and that the person called must be signed in too; on other devices a FaceTime link is joined from a browser with no login necessary, and Group FaceTime may not be available in all countries or regions.

products.description: End-to-end encrypted by default, including group calls. A caller needs an Apple Account, and Apple's page on FaceTime links describes creating one from an iPhone, iPad, iPod touch or Mac, after which anyone can join from a browser.

products.name: Microsoft Teams (free)

privacy.note: Microsoft's support page says end-to-end encryption for Teams meetings is part of Teams Premium, an add-on licence, and can be used when an IT admin has enabled it; during an end-to-end encrypted meeting recording, live captions and transcription are unavailable.

openness.note: The Microsoft Services Agreement, which has a section for Skype, Microsoft Teams and GroupMe, says users may not disassemble, decompile, decrypt, hack, emulate, exploit or reverse engineer any software or other aspect of the Services.

accessibility.note: Microsoft's support page says a Teams meeting can be joined from any device without signing into a Teams account, that no app install is needed, and that Teams for web works on Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome.

economical.note: Microsoft's support page lists Teams Free meetings as up to 60 minutes with 100 participants; Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscriptions raise this to 30 hours and 300 participants.

products.description: The successor Microsoft recommends to Skype users. Guests can join in a browser without an account, but Microsoft's page puts end-to-end encryption in the paid Teams Premium add-on and says an administrator must enable it.

products.name: WhatsApp calls

privacy.note: WhatsApp's calling page says 'Your calls on WhatsApp are always end-to-end encrypted' and describes both one-on-one and group calling.

openness.note: The European Commission's Digital Markets Act portal says WhatsApp and Messenger must support end-to-end voice and video calls with third-party messaging services by 7 September 2027, the third phase of the interoperability duty.

accessibility.note: WhatsApp's calling page says calls work across iOS, Android and web, with Mac, iPad and Windows apps, and that group calls can hold up to 32 people.

economical.note: WhatsApp's calling page says video and voice calls are free and have no time limits, and adds that data charges may apply.

links.label: Call interoperability duty under the DMA

products.description: Always end-to-end encrypted, free with no time limit, and available on phones, desktops and the web. It belongs to Meta.

products.name: Discord voice and video

privacy.note: Discord's May 2026 announcement says every voice and video call, whether in DMs, group DMs, voice channels or Go Live streams, is end-to-end encrypted by default with no opt-in, that stage channels are excluded, and that it has no current plans to extend end-to-end encryption to text messages.

openness.note: Discord's May 2026 announcement says the DAVE call-encryption protocol is open, that its implementation is open source, and that Trail of Bits audited it; the announcement does not describe the Discord apps as open source.

accessibility.note: Discord's download page lists apps for Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android and consoles.

economical.note: Discord's Nitro page sells Nitro Basic at $2.99 a month and Nitro at $9.99 a month as upgrades, and lists HD streaming among the Nitro perks.

products.description: Discord says every voice and video call outside stage channels is now end-to-end encrypted, and the encryption protocol is published and audited. Text messages are not covered by that encryption.

products.name: Webex (free plan)

privacy.note: Cisco's help page says end-to-end encrypted meetings are chosen with the 'E2E Encryption + Identity' meeting type, that a person must change their preferences to make all meetings encrypted by default, and that scheduled meetings, space meetings and Personal Room meetings in the Webex App support it.

accessibility.note: Cisco's help article for the free plan says a free Webex account hosts the meetings and recommends downloading the desktop app for more features; the article does not say whether guests need an account.

economical.note: Cisco's help article says the free plan hosts meetings of up to 40 minutes with up to 100 attendees and includes unlimited messaging and calling with other Webex users.

products.description: A Cisco meeting tool with a free tier of 40-minute meetings for up to 100 people. End-to-end encryption is available per meeting, but a host has to choose it, and it is not the default.

products.name: Signal calls

privacy.note: Signal's legal page says Signal cannot decrypt or otherwise access the content of messages or calls, and that the technical data it keeps is limited to the minimum needed to run the service, such as authentication tokens, keys and push tokens.

openness.note: Signal's calling library RingRTC is public on GitHub under the signalapp organisation and is licensed AGPLv3 only.

accessibility.note: Signal's November 2024 call-links post says a link can be shared with anyone on Signal, who can join the call in a tap or click with no group chat required.

economical.note: Signal's home page says the app is an independent nonprofit supported by grants and donations, with no ads, affiliate marketers or trackers.

products.description: Every call is end-to-end encrypted, the calling code is public, and the app is free and run by a nonprofit. Signal's legal page says an account is registered with a phone number, so a guest has to be on Signal too.

products.name: Jitsi Meet

privacy.note: Jitsi's security page says end-to-end encryption is not on by default and is switched on with a toggle in the Security options, works in Chromium-based browsers 83 and above and the Electron client, and covers audio, video and screen sharing but not chat or polls; without it, traffic is encrypted with DTLS-SRTP on the network but is decrypted in the videobridge's memory while being routed.

openness.note: The jitsi-meet repository describes Jitsi Meet as a set of open source projects, and GitHub lists its licence as Apache-2.0.

accessibility.note: Jitsi's handbook says people can join by following a link, and that on the public meet.jit.si server the first person to join must authenticate with a Google, Facebook or GitHub account or wait for a moderator.

economical.note: jitsi.org describes the service as completely free video conferencing; the pages read state no meeting-length cap.

products.description: Open source, free, and joinable from a link without an account. Calls are not end-to-end encrypted unless a participant switches that on, and the public server has required hosts to sign in with Google, Facebook or GitHub since August 2023.

products.name: Element Call

privacy.note: The Element Call repository lists end-to-end encryption among its key features, describing secure and private calls over the Matrix protocol.

openness.note: The Element Call repository says the software is dual-licensed by New Vector Ltd (Element), usable for free under the GNU Affero General Public License version 3 or under a paid Element Commercial License.

accessibility.note: The Element Call repository says it runs as a standalone app connected to a Matrix homeserver with a login interface, or as a widget inside a Matrix client; it does not describe joining without an account.

economical.note: Element's pricing page lists a free Community edition for non-professional self-hosted deployments that includes Element Call and a free app, with Enterprise and Sovereign tiers priced per deployment.

products.description: Federated calling on the Matrix protocol, listed as end-to-end encrypted, with public source. The way in is a Matrix account on a homeserver, so it suits groups that already use Matrix.

products.name: Whereby

privacy.note: Whereby's security page says end-to-end encryption is in effect for small rooms, that for large rooms encrypted media is decrypted only in server memory, that it does not store video and audio data, and that it relies mostly on AWS in Dublin.

accessibility.note: Whereby's Meetings page says guests need no downloads and no login, and that calls run in the browser.

economical.note: Whereby's plans page lists the Free plan as one room URL, 4 attendees per meeting and meetings of up to 30 minutes; the Pro plan at $10.99 a month raises this to 100 attendees with no time limit.

products.description: The easiest for a guest, because nothing is installed and no login is asked, and end-to-end encrypted in small rooms. The free plan is small, at 4 people for 30 minutes, and large rooms are decrypted in server memory.

products.name: Jami

privacy.note: Jami's site says all communications are peer-to-peer and end-to-end encrypted with perfect forward secrecy, and that no personal information is required to create an account.

openness.note: Jami's site says it is a GNU project backed by the Free Software Foundation and licensed under GNU GPLv3 or later.

accessibility.note: Jami's site lists apps for Linux, Android, Android TV, Windows, macOS and iOS and says no personal information is needed to create an account; it does not describe a way for a guest to join without Jami.

economical.note: Jami's site says the software is free, unlimited without restriction on bandwidth, number of accounts or features, and that there will never be advertising.

products.description: A peer-to-peer GNU project with no server relaying data between users, end-to-end encryption on everything, and no personal details needed for an account. The site describes no way for a guest to join without Jami.

products.name: Threema Private

privacy.note: Threema's Private product page lists end-to-end encrypted voice, video and group calls, and says every message, call and shared file is protected.

openness.note: Threema's Android app repository on GitHub is licensed AGPL-3.0.

accessibility.note: Threema's pricing page describes Threema Private as available on all platforms and usable anonymously.

economical.note: Threema's pricing page lists Threema Private at 6.00 as a one-time price, with the currency and amount depending on the app store and country.

products.description: Swiss, paid once, with end-to-end encrypted voice, video and group calls and no phone number needed. The purchase is a real barrier next to free apps.

products.name: Nextcloud Talk

privacy.note: The Talk 21 changelog lists end-to-end encryption for calls with the high-performance backend, and later entries block mobile clients when it is enabled, which describes an option an administrator turns on.

openness.note: The spreed repository, which holds Nextcloud Talk's source, is licensed AGPL-3.0.

accessibility.note: Nextcloud's Talk page offers self-hosting or a free account at a provider, and says a lobby lets guests wait until the call starts.

economical.note: Nextcloud's Talk page points to a free account at a provider or the server software for self-hosting.

products.description: Video calls inside a Nextcloud server you run or rent, with public source. End-to-end encryption for calls exists as an administrator option and is blocked on mobile clients when enabled, and guests wait in a lobby until the call starts.
